J. L. Austin is called a naive empiricist because his ordinary-language method treats “what we should say when,” gathered case by case, as philosophy’s basic evidence. He held that cataloguing those distinctions would dissolve traditional problems, as in *A Plea for Excuses*, *Sense and Sensibilia*, and *How to Do Things with Words*. “Naive” marks the assumption that ordinary usage is straightforward, theory-neutral data and that description alone can settle the questions.
